p: Sergeants?
Alright, please let’s mute all the zooms.
[inaudible] but that should close at like six o’clock.
Yeah, that’s what I’m saying. That’s why–
[interposing] Please mute yourself if you’re on Zoom.

Hopefully they’ll make it by six. Local Law 92 from 2023, there was a resource navigator program for women, transgender, intersex, non-binary, and gender non-conforming people. Is this resource navigator program fully operational and fulfilling its mandate?
We do have within our reentry services resource navigation, and then also we have on our website the ability to go in and search for those services, yes.
Okay. And what budget line item is this program included under?
I don’t think we– I think we were able to do it in a budget neutral way.
I’m sorry, can you bring the mic a little bit closer? Sorry, I’m going deaf.
I’ll turn it over to our
I believe the budget item is included under our reentry budget.
Under reentry? Okay. Okay. Those are my questions, Chair. Thank you.

Thank you so much. A few more questions. A question about the Intensive Case Management pilot. This is a pre-trial supervised release program that provides case workers to those that– who check in and also offer services and provide reminders to people of their court dates and other things. Does the Preliminary Budget include funding to expand on this, or is that something that there’s a planned cut on that program?

Chair, currently the funding is maintained for fiscal year ‘26 at $9 million. There is not an out-year funding at the moment, but we continue to work with OMB to assess the program needs and the fiscal needs to continue the program.

Alright. Similar question, but I guess on the issue of District Attorneys, what steps is MOCJ taking to ensure that District Attorneys and defenders have installed technology so they can process, store and share evidence efficiently? And also, the state approved $50 million for this two years ago. Do we have any

information on when this will be installed and finalized?

So, in working with the DAs, we talk to them about needs and where they are with the discovery. The discovery funding that the state provided went directly to the District Attorneys, and so they are– they managed what they spent those funds on in terms of the technology and their infrastructure bills. Given that each office has its own separate infrastructure, it’s our understanding that they’re in different places and that they are diligently working to get a place of having their systems completed, but we understand that the Bronx started sooner with one of the vendors and may be in a better place to be moving through what the technology looks like. Queens had its own internal database system that it was building out. Manhattan also has a good infrastructure system that it was building out. Staten Island was using a product that was on the state level, be it used by other prosecutors across New York State.

And Brooklyn also is looking at building up its infrastructure. So, each one of them is in a different place and we continuously work with them as well as the Corporation Counsel where there may be challenges with contracting to ensure that they are– resources are being appropriately dedicated towards the technology bills and any challenges are addressed.

Alright. And last question for me: Can you talk to us about some of the criminal justice housing related programs that you have. I know you provide transitional housing for those exiting Rikers. Can you talk about those housing programs a little bit?

Sure. It's our emergency and transitional housing program. We work with three providers to implement that program. It’s the Fortune Society, Housing Works, and Housing Plus which is a consortium for women. And we have about 800 beds open now, and we’re planning for about 150– about a 150 more over the next year.

Alright. Thank you so much. Anyone else has any other questions? Alright, so I

think this concludes this part this of the– Actually, Council Member Wong has a–
[interposing] I’ll squeeze in a question. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Chair. I noticed that you offer services for defendants as well as services for victims. Is that right? No? I’m wrong?
Not quite. We do have some services for victims, yes.
So, how do you balance it because they seem to be, you know, conflicting goals here?

Well, most of the contracts for victim services sit with HRA now. However, we believe that the criminal justice system is– the criminal legal system is a continuum, and everybody needs to– we’re looking at public safety. It helps us both to ensure that victims have what they need and then ensure that people are less likely to reenter the system. So, that’s how we sort of balance the concept.

Thank you, Council Member Wong. And I also want to just highlight the fact that we

are– our community courts deal a lot of work with restorative justice. So that means that instead of looking at a punitive model meaning you did something bad, and so now we’re going to punish you, and the person who was harmed doesn’t necessarily get the justice that they’re seeking. So, restorative models allow both the individual that was harmed and the individual that did the harm to work together to think about what healing really looks like. Because healing doesn’t always mean that we have to put somebody in jail. Healing can be what do I need to do to try to bring you back to the place you were before I did this harm to you, and working together, the person who was harmed and the person who did to the harm come to a resolution as to how the two of them walk away from that scenario stronger and better for the interaction and community is stronger at that point as well.
Okay. Thank you for clarifying.

Thank you. Thank you so much again for joining us today. We look forward to

continuing the conversation on the many topics that we have talked about today, and thank you for the work you do.
Thank you.

Alright. Now we’ll be opening the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. This hearing is already being recorded. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today’s hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you’ll have two minutes to speak on today’s oversight hearing topic, the budgets of the New York City

Police Department, District Attorneys, CCRB, and MOCJ, the Mayor’s Office of Criminal Justice. If you have a written statement or additional testimony you’d like to submit on the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. For in-person panelists please come to the table once your name has been called. I’ll now call the first panel, in-person panel, who has already joined: Tina Luongo from the Legal Aid Society, Piyali Basak from the Neighborhood Defender Services, Juval Scott from the Bronx Defenders, Stan German from the New York County Defender Services, and Lisa Schreibersdorf from the Brooklyn Defender Services. So, I guess we can start from left to right, or do you want to start from right to left?
We have an order, so we’re going to go– if it’s okay, we’ll go this way.

Sounds good. And we’ll provide Council Members with four minutes of

questions. For this panel, we’ll provide five minutes for the opening statement. Thank you.

Thank you. Good afternoon Council Members and Chair. My name is Stan German. I’m the Executive Director for New York County Defender Services. Today’s March 18th, in the defender community and courts throughout the country, this is known as Gideon’s Day. 63 years ago the Supreme Court issued the ruling in Gideon V. Wainwright that essentially poor people accused of crimes have the right to counsel, and I’m hoping that’s an omen that in this budget year we are going to see the kind of budgets that reflect the value that all our public defender offices and our staff bring to the criminal legal system. The reality is that in terms of a marketplace, New York City is simply not competitive with the rest of the country. When you look at jurisdictions in large cities like Los Angeles, Atlanta, Seattle, Oakland, San Francisco, all of them have starting salaries for public defenders north of $105,000. When you look at federal defenders who are public defenders in the federal system throughout the country, they have a similar starting salary.

If you look at upstate counties in New York State, closer to home, there are seven counties upstate with a lower cost of living where the starting salary is at $100,000 or less. And if you take into account the cost of living adjustments for cities like Minneapolis and Houston, they are also north of $100,000. New York City continues to lag behind. Now, on the issue of affordability, we’ve been talking about this issue long before it became a mayoral hot topic last year. We’ve been coming to this chamber year after year after year talking about affordability, and the struggles that our staff have in making a livable wage in New York City. You have law students who are graduating with six-figure student loan debts, and yet they choose– they choose to not go into the private sector, but serve the public. We have got to do better by our staff. You’ve asked a lot of questions today, Chair, about ATIs, alternatives to incarceration. You asked MOCJ and you asked the DAs. The reality is that work in large part gets done by the social workers in our offices. That takes preparing clients, discharge

planning, finding drug programs, finding a place to sleep, going through the diversion process at the different DAs offices. It's our staff that are navigating all of that space, and all of us collectively, we need more resources for more social workers. We are not going to close Rikers Island unless we have the kind of social services that the clients are going to need so that we can safely reduce the jail population at Rikers Island. Closer to home, I just want to do a comparison, because you know, at the end of the day, a budget is a value statement. It tells New Yorkers what this chamber values. And over the past four years with the prior administration, a clear value statement was set. N YPD salaries went up significantly. A five-year police officer with minimal overtime makes $150,000 per year. A public defender by contrast it would take them 20 years to make $150,000. The retention problem is real. Our staff are forced to choose between do I have a child and incur all the expenses with child care, or do I stay as a public defender? And what we see increasingly is of course they’re

leaving our offices, whether it’s to buy a home or to start a family. When you lose that experience, again, case processing takes a hit. A more senior lawyer can adjudicate a case more quickly than a younger attorney who’s learning the process. All of this we can tie into our mandate to close Rikers Island, and we need budget increases which my colleagues will address specifically in order to make that happen. Thank you.

Good afternoon and thank you very much, Chair Feliz, and thank you, Council Member Wong, for staying. I’m Tina Luongo. I’m the Chief Defender at the Legal Aid Society. I've been practicing as a public defender in this new– in this city since 2002. Let me start where this actually lives, in the real lives of the people we serve and the people who will likely come as the members of the public to testify about their needs. When New Yorkers are in crisis– New Yorkers are in crisis, when someone’s arrested, when a parent is at risk of losing a child or a child is accused of a crime, when a family's rent is due and a court date is missed because of

work, when a person is terrified about what one mistake could mean for their figure, public defenders and our interdisciplinary teams are the people closest to what is needed and they are closest to where the solutions lie. But here's the hard truth. The City cannot keep asking our teams to carry more crisis, more complexity,and more responsibility while failing to sustain the workforce that makes those outcomes possible. So I want to be clear about what we are asking today and why it can no longer wait yet another fiscal year. We need an infusion into our funding streams above about $100 million to fully support and allow us to be able to work with our staff, many of them unionized, many of them in this audience, many of them watching online who do this work every day so that we can do what actually Stan has just said. Because the reality of this situation is if we don’t, we are not just failing them, we are failing the people who are dragged every day into the criminal legal system, the family separation system and the immigration detention system. Because that is who is at the heart of representing clients and representing those families to turn the system around.

In addition to that $100 million, right now it is critically important to fund immigration representation, and there’s a lot talk in a separate hearing that covers that type of funding for our immigration units, but there is a specific unit in our offices that does work pursuant to the constitution under a case Kentucky V. Padilla [sp?] that indicates that as public defenders, as criminal defense lawyers, we must advise our clients who are in the criminal legal system of adverse immigration consequences. And now more than ever it is critical that we build bigger teams because frankly what we’re falling right now is an increase of the harms given the federal actions across the country and specifically in our city. And then my colleagues will talk about the fact that we need real change in our contracting process, because the way in which our monies flow and the monies flow to other nonprofits. It’s very different than how the money flows to the District Attorneys. And that creates lag times and cash flow issues that are real. So, I turn this now to my colleagues to go more into depth, but this is what's at stake. I’m asking

that we treat our public defenders and our staff the way New York treats other essential services as a core infrastructure that is absolutely critical, and if we do not address this, our attrition will continue and all the things we talked about, about moving and case processing will simply not be available, because at the heart of it is the public defender who needs to represent that person in court. Thank you.

Sorry about that. Good afternoon. My name is Juval Scott. I’m the Executive Director of the Bronx Defenders. Unlike my colleagues I don’t have a career practicing in New York. I came from the federal defender system, and so I’ve been the Executive Director for about 19 months. I’ll admit that as I start these comments, I’m a bit, you know, uncertain of where to begin, because I believe that if we were here to have a serious conversation that we would be treated in a similar way as the District Attorneys, and we would have meaningful conversation, and we would have a panel that was dedicated and allocated to us. And the reason why that would happen is because there’s no way that you increase prosecutions.

There’s no way that you can have a serious inquiry about what prosecutors need without critical understanding of what the constitutional counterpart to the prosecutor’s office is, and that’s public defenders. Today is National Public Defender Day, and today I got to watch the prosecutors praise the City Council for increasing salaries for their staff, making it more comfortable for them to do the work that– the other side of the work that my– the people in my office do. But we’re not able to offer that same praise, because year after year as I understand it, before I got here and even since I’ve been here, we continue to ask City Council, the City, to increase funding for the salary and benefits lines for public defenders in New York City. It is true that federal defenders in New York City make a considerable amount more than public defenders in our offices. Public defenders at about 10 years in the federal defender system make about $196,000. That is far more than what the public defenders in our offices make. But if you look at

cities that are comparable to New York, even that is low. The lowest salary for public defenders in comparable California cities is $134,000 a year. That’s to start right out of law school. That is the starting rate, and the reason why that is meaningful is because it allows young people to come in to focus on the work so that they can do critical work on behalf of the people that we represent, the community that we serve so that they can gain the skills and training and assets needed to do work at the highest level, and so they stay in the work, and so that we’re not constantly having to retrain new people year after year and not keeping institutional knowledge so that people who do come in as new attorneys are able to benefit from their colleagues who remain in the offices. That’s what makes a public defender office great. That’s what makes public defense a sustainable pathway, a career pathway, in large and major cities. And so we ask the city– you know, we ask the City Council as we do every year to increase significantly the salaries on behalf of public defenders. It’s the only way to make the work sustainable. It’s the only

way that we can continue to recruit. And we’d note that people who do this privately and are appointed on cases get paid considerably more than our staff. So, you know, paying institutional providers additional money still realized a cost savings for the city. And so we really would ask that you think about what it means for people to dedicate their career to representing the community’s most vulnerable citizens, and to really think about what it means for them to have to weight whether or not they can pay their bills as they do this work and focus on– they should be able to focus on the work. We ask a lot of our employees, and so we’re asking for you to increase the money that we’re able to pay them and the benefits lines, because it’s not keeping pace. Health care benefits are going up across the board. All benefits are going up and we need to be able to meet the moment, because that is our constitutional mandate. Thank you.

Hi, I’m Lisa Schreibersdorf. I’m the Executive Director of Brooklyn Defender Services. We represent people in Brooklyn and Queens. I interview dozens of people

each year who make the commitment to bring their skills, dedication and talent to helping people who get arrested. When people are arrested, they face a wide variety of lifelong consequences such as loss of educational opportunities, loss of employment, eviction from housing, deportation, and many other harms. Each of these is the responsibility of that person’s attorney, their criminal defense attorney. No matter the seriousness of the underlying case, the impact on the people we represent is wide and deep, and the staff that do this work give themselves to the work, including the support that is needed to deal with these issues, along with things that are affecting our clients such as drug and alcohol use, mental illness, physical illness, impairment, disability, trauma, and poverty. Despite their good work, many of my staff do not have sufficient money to pay their own rent, pay their own utilities, and certainly not to keep up with their student loans. My office is scheduled to conduct collective bargaining this year, and the staff is understandably frustrated that year-in and year-out they come to me

as their leader and just want to be paid a wage that corresponds with the other big cities and which can provide them with a living wage. All of them have given up the financial benefits of working at corporate law firms or even other types of legal work that can be a lot more lucrative. And while they do this important work for the individuals we serve as well as honestly for our very democracy, they are devalued over and over by the city, the city that they call home and the city to which they have devoted themselves. It is not surprising that this has a significant impact on the morale of the office. It is not surprising that people lose hope, not only for themselves, but for their clients and for the systems that they are facing every single day. The issue is a crisis beyond the individual employee who well-deserves this raise. It is existential and now is the time to show that it will end. The progress will be made that there is a commitment by this Council to pay the essential workers that we are. To do that, we must focus a little bit on some boring wonky stuff which is always my assignment.

You’ll get used to that. That’s the procurement process. Unlike our counterparts at the DA’s office, we are not government agencies. We are not elected officials. We are not blessed with free rent, good pensions for our staff or the resources of the entire NYPD, the Medical Examiner’s Office, to work on our cases. We are nonprofits with a contract with the City of New York, and due to that, we are bound to procurement rules that include bidding for our work on a regular basis. And often, the financial barriers that also incumber other nonprofits that are providing an entirely different type of service. The next RFP already are overdue. Our process- RFP process and it’s overdue. It may come out this September for the next fiscal year. It may be delayed again. During these in-between years, the City has historically not provided a real avenue to address specific funding shortfalls which makes it really critical to assure that when this comes out, when this RFP comes out, it has to have the proper amount of funding. And in order to give our staff the salaries that reflect their value and that are competitive, we

estimate as you heard earlier, it’s about $100 million just for staff funding. We have thousands of people working for us. That needs to be added to the RFP. We can’t just talk about it. It needs to be funded before that process begins. That also does not include increases in rent, need for more space which we all have, increases in health insurance, and just about every other everyday item that is part of our budget like pens or computers. We are asking that you please fight for that RFP this year so that our boring and burdensome– yes, I wrote that down as I was sitting here all day– our burdensome procurement process is fruitful and results in a meaningful use of our resources and time. Thank you very much.

Good afternoon, Council. My name is Piyali Basak. I’m the Managing Director for the Neighborhood Defender Service in Harlem. I wholeheartedly join my colleagues in this request for increased funding to support our offices, especially so that we can provide increased salaries. I have until about a year ago I was a public defender before I was in this role representing clients, and I can tell you every single one of our colleagues of our

staff who come into this work come into it with a commitment to serve our communities. And I hope the Council honors that commitment. But I want to focus on our request for additional funding to increase Padilla teams. Immigration Law is complex and subject to the abrupt, dramatic shifts sometimes changing the legal consequences of a criminal case over night. There’s a great deal of nuance and understanding. To understand the status of an individual person based on their history, as well as a specific impact of a plea bargain. Given the high court mandate and the necessity to provide accurate, up-to-date, specialized immigration advice, our offices have hired Padilla attorneys, dedicated attorneys providing this advice. Over the past year, increased ICE presences– and I’m sure I don’t need to educate the Council about that– has created a sharp uptick in the need for our Padilla attorneys. Our staff had to devote significant time and resources to tracking daily policy changes, court rulings, enforcement practices while also trying to provide clear guidance to our teams.

Our non-citizen clients, they’re terrified. Even those with lawful status face a possibility that even a minor criminal offense can lead to detention and separation and permanent exile from the United States. Our clients require more direct contact and support, and we try to do so by offering that, by providing the social support as well as connection to other resources. We’re constantly monitoring the Department of Correction’s actions, and for clients who have state, we’re providing court and guidance when it’s needed. We help connect them to attorneys, and we are also constantly providing access to our clients, to immigration teams who are receiving nonstop calls about check-ins with immigration authorities and questions about ICE presence at schools and homes, and other concerns they might have. And so we are asking the Council for additional funding and $10 million to our overall budget so that MOCJ can distribute these funds to our offices. This sustained and expanded funding for this unit will allow us to continue providing this essential

guidance, responding to the increasing complexity of these immigration cases. Thank you.

Alright. Thank you all for being here. Thank you for your testimony and also for all the work you do for our city and the people of this city, especially those that are under some of their most vulnerable positions. So, I have a few questions about salary, retention, and then funding. Salary– I used to be a tenant attorney for Bronx Legal Services. The same issues that all of you mentioned I saw at basically the office training new lawyers, law school graduates generally, spending lots of resources training them, and then two years later they lose them. So they have to start all over which, you know, obviously not a good system. So, on that issue, what would be– what do you think should be, I guess, the proper starting salary, and also how much funding would it require to get there. I think I heard $100 million, but I just want to make sure that I’m putting that on the right issue.

And I think Stan mentioned it, that, look, a starting salary for somebody up in Schenectady, New York, was a $102,000. So, if you

look at that as a benchmark. Certainly we believe that we have to at a minimum look at our upstate counties and come to– but that– think about that, because you have to factor in cost of living. But at some point, we have to be realistic that $100,000 starting salary is something that we should start to think about and implement. And then realize that there have to be consistent cost of living increases to keep pace with inflation. What my colleague Lisa testified to is when our contracts are held flat year after year during our comp– sixth year and now upwards of eight years of contract. Because we are nonprofits, if our rent goes up, if our health care goes up, the only– we don’t get extra money and so then you have to start then thinking about how am I making a choice as a manager to have to both increase the salary which is what we need, or not then pay the increase in the rent on the space we need. My colleagues in the District Attorney offices do not have that problem, do not have that problem. And so it’s not only about the starting salary, but then it is about experience. We talked a lot about case processing and that really is about for us, not about

cases, but about people, our clients. And so if you have an attorney who is taking on a serious case where someone is incarcerated, and they leave because they can’t afford it any longer. That client has to get transferred to another lawyer, and that lawyer cannot pick up the case, that case, and meet that client and run off to trial. They now need to take the time to relearn everything and build a relationship. And I have had a situation where clients are in– at Rikers on serious chargers, and in the span of that case, two attorneys have left the office. Now, it’s not their fault. They were just that breaking point. So, besides starting salary, we must look at the experience and what it means to keep experienced attorneys in our office.

I just want to put some actual like hard numbers. You heard $100 million for salaries– would get us 200,000 starting point, maybe a little more which is what we really need, but also help us get raises across the years and including also our supervisors and other people to train all the new people, but I think there probably needs to be about another $50 million, I’m guessing.

And again, none of us really know, but if you’re asking for a specific number, we– when this RFP comes out, it probably needs to have exactly what it, you know, what it’s currently funded at, which is hard for any of us to glean out of the budget. Let’s be real about it. Plus $150 million, and that should be part of the procurement process where each of us can then go to MOCJ and explain exactly how we plan to use the money that, you know, we need to do this, and I feel like if that amount got into our, you know, into the flow, it could make a really big difference.

And I would just tag onto that. I’d be remiss if I didn’t just note that the $100,000 figure that they’re tossing out is the floor, not the ceiling. That’s still too low. I just want to make sure that I’m crystal clear there, and also when we’re making the comparison to prosecutors salary city, attorney salaries, keep in mind that what we– you know, our– the pension that they get, we don’t get. So it’s still not parity. Even if the salaries were the exact same or even a little bit more, they’re still not parity. The benefits that you get in working for the city are distinctly different, and

so I just want to be clear. We’re here asking for a lot of money. We’re going to keep asking for money until it's fair.

Would all of you mind sharing the– I guess the starting salary for, I guess, a lawyer at your office? What’s the general starting salary or ballpark? I know for legal services it was like $70-80,000 for those that passed–
[interposing] Yeah, right now this year we’re at $88,000.
A law graduate waiting to be admitted starts at $84,000.
I think my office is right at $90, because we actually gave people raises last year, and you know, and for -what other things like space in order to do that.
We’re also at $84,000 and also we'll be bargaining this year.

Okay. Has the– I guess the retention issue or lack of funding issue, has that led to inability to properly handle cases, including giving them the time and attention that they deserve, including on criminal cases?

Obviously, people have their– defendants have the right to– constitutional right to a lawyer. So what are some of the effects that this has had on that?

I mean, to be clear, no client has shouldered the burden of our burnout. The folks who shouldered the burden are the attorneys and the social workers who remain in the offices who then have to step up and get that work done. And so, Tina just alluded to it. You have an attorney who’s at five years with 70 cases. That person leaves, right, those cases have to be reassigned. They’re assigned in some cases to supervisors, other attorneys, and then their caseloads just went up. So the work is absolutely being done in all our offices. It’s being done at an extremely high level, but the cost is the increasing burnout of our staff, and you just alluded to it. Then we get younger. We have to train all over again, and we’re just– it’s like bailing water, you know, out of a sinking ship. We’re just always struggling to get above board. But client representation and the work always gets done.

Just to add to that, I think what we’re seeing is, again, attorneys leaving about years five, six, seven out, who are starting families who cannot afford the public defender salary to support their families. It’s not just, you know, cases being transferred. It’s a mentorship that gets offered, and it’s so critical as part of the training. It’s sometimes supervisors themselves which that is so hard to replace. We have to train to become a supervisor, but they cannot stay on even with the salary bumps that they get which is, you know, frankly not substantial. We need– we would like to do better. So, it is– that is a huge loss for our offices to have experience and sharing that experience among the staff, because that’s where people learn from.

I would quickly add along to that, one of the trends that you see in public defense at about that mark is that you start to lose a lot of the attorneys of color. So, Black attorneys, Black male attorneys in particular as they want to start families, but other attorneys of color really can’t afford to stay in

public defense, and so it becomes an equity issue. It creates– it really creates a situation where you have no pipeline of Black and Brown people to become supervisors and mentors in offices to ascend to leadership to be able to take on the mantle. And so when you have new, young attorneys of color, people of color come into the office and there’s no leadership that looks like them, they don’t have– you know, you don’t see yourself, right, in the leadership, and so you don’t really see that pathway. You don’t see the longevity in the field, and what that means in the Bronx especially where the bulk of our clients are, you know, Black and Brown, it means that our– the people that we serve don’t see people who look like them representing them. And so it becomes an information gap of sorts. There are things culturally that get lost because, you know, the attorneys don’t necessarily relate to the people that we serve, and then also those conversations are missing in an office. And so, I just want to highlight that equity issue as well, because it’s important. I think it’s something that gets overlooked a lot.

Okay. Has the staffing and retention issue created issues related to case-related delays? For example, lawyers not having enough time. They have to adjourn, so a criminal case gets adjourned, delayed and then adjourned again and delayed?

Yeah, it’s very similar to what we spoke about. One, you have to now assume a colleague who left caseload. You now have that burden. And what happens? As much as you try not to, you have to now triage. You also– it has the effect on the person who is now– who’s the client. They built a relationship with somebody in a situation may I say, where trust is not given often because there should be mistrust because this person is accused and being prosecuted. And we are paid, right, by the same government that is prosecuting them. So building trust is something that our staff has to work very hard to do. And now you are held at Rikers and you get a visit and it’s a different attorney than you know and now trust, and now it starts all over again.

So you have actual what we call case processing issues, but more importantly, you have real value issues there that we have to address in New York City. And I want to say just one more thing about sort of what the effect of attrition is. investigations. Over the years, mayors have strengthened DOI's authority through several mayoral executive orders, most notably in the late 1970s through the mid-1980s. Those executive orders give DOI the authority to access most City records, emails, and other documents without a subpoena, and to compel interviews of City employees and vendors. The executive orders also mandate that all City employees who become aware of suspected corruption or fraud must report it directly and promptly to DOI or risk discipline. DOI has the power to subpoena third parties, non-City employees, for documents and for testimony, which DOI is authorized to take under oath. A mayoral executive order in the mid-1980s reorganized DOI to its current structure, with Inspectors General reporting to the DOI Commissioner. This shift removed mayoral agency oversight of Inspectors General and provided DOI with an important measure of independence, establishing DOI as the City agency responsible for combating City-related corruption. DOI's investigations and factual findings can lead to criminal prosecutions, disciplinary proceedings, and other administrative actions. Our

staff has deep knowledge of government operations and its complexities, and the many ways that corruption can creep into City government, thereby undermining access to City services and siphoning precious public funds. Based on our investigations, DOI makes recommendations for policy and procedural reforms to City agencies to address corruption, vulnerabilities, and prevent misconduct from reoccurring. DOI also issues public reports that have significant impact in New York City. These public reports discuss DOI's factual findings and our reasoning for the recommendations that we issue. In addition to criminal and disciplinary investigations, DOI investigates potential conflicts of interest that may result in referrals to Conflicts of Interest Board, as well as claims of retaliation against employees of agencies and City contractors who report misconduct and are protected by the City's whistleblower law. DOI also provides other critical services to the City, including background investigations for certain City employees, vendor name checks for City-funded vendors, and integrity monitoring services for large City projects, and to rehabilitate needed vendors with integrity concerns.

DOI's work saves the City money by preventing fraud, identifying waste, and receiving millions of dollars in asset forfeiture and restitution funds that are collected as a result of some of our investigations. DOI's investigations in Calendar Year 2025 have covered a broad range of areas, from strengthening the safety of young people in the City's care, protecting public funds, and tackling crimes that compromise New Yorkers' access to essential needs such as housing and wages. DOI issued 14 public reports and saved more than 5 million dollars for the City through DOI's monitorship of the asylum seeker contracts. In addition, DOI investigations led to the collection of more than 6 million dollars in financial recoveries to the City. DOI made 174 arrests, fielded nearly 13,000 complaints, provided corruption prevention training to more than 37,000 City employees, and others through our digital learning module, webinars, and in-person lectures, and issued 113 policy and procedure recommendations to improve City operations and best practices. In past years, DOI has leveraged State and Federal asset forfeiture to supplement our needs in this area, but at the current rate of spending, forfeiture reserves are projected to be depleted by Fiscal Year '28. Let me provide some background on how we receive forfeiture funding and the legal rules for using it. Forfeiture funding is intended to supplement DOI's resources and expand its investigative capacities, not to pay for ordinary expenditures that should be appropriately funded by the City. DOI receives forfeiture from its criminal investigations. Both federal and state laws provide for the seizure of assets that are connected to criminal activity and the subsequent sharing of those funds with the investigative agencies responsible for the investigations. Forfeiture funds must be used to support legitimate law enforcement activities. The majority of our forfeiture funds come from federal prosecutions, and there are very strict Department of Justice guidelines on how forfeiture funds can be used and for what purposes. The DOJ guidelines

require that forfeiture funds supplement, not supplant, DOI budget. This means that the City cannot reduce DOI's budget due to the ability of forfeiture funds. Investigations do not always result in forfeiture funding to DOI, and there is no way to predict how much forfeiture DOI will receive in any given year.
